title: Ride hailing
summary: High-rate location updates, matching and trip state.
prompt: Design the core of a ride-hailing service: drivers stream their location, riders request a ride and are matched with a nearby driver, and both follow the trip live.

requirements: Functional: driver location updates, ride request, matching and offer/accept, live trip tracking, fare at trip end.
Non-functional: matching within seconds; a driver is never assigned two trips; location data can be slightly stale; city-level failure isolation.
estimation: 1M active drivers sending a location every 4 s ⇒ 250,000 updates/s.
Each update ~100 bytes ⇒ 25 MB/s; keep only the latest position hot and sample history to cold storage.
10M trips a day ≈ 115 requests/s average, with strong peaks by city and time.
api: Driver: a persistent connection sending {lat, lng, heading, status}; receives offers.
Rider: POST /rides {pickup, dropoff} → {rideId, status}; subscribe to ride updates.
POST /rides/{id}/accept by driver; conditional on the ride still being unassigned.
data: Driver locations: in-memory geo index (geohash or S2 cells) partitioned by city, entries expire if updates stop.
rides(ride_id, rider_id, driver_id, status, version, …) in a strongly consistent store, with a state machine requested → offered → accepted → started → completed.
Location history sampled into a stream for ETAs, fraud and disputes.
design: Location service ingests updates, updates the city’s geo index and publishes to trip subscribers.
Matching service queries nearby available drivers, ranks by ETA (not straight-line distance), and offers to one driver at a time with a short timeout.
Trip service owns ride state with conditional updates; riders get pushed updates of the driver’s position.
deepDives: No double assignment: accept is a conditional update on both the ride (status = offered to this driver) and the driver (status = available), in one transaction or with a driver-level lock.
Offer strategy: sequential offers avoid conflicts but are slower; parallel offers to a few drivers are faster but need the conditional accept to pick a winner.
Partition by city or region: matching is local, failures are contained, and hot cities can be split into zones.
bottlenecks: Update rate: keep latest locations only in memory, batch writes to history, and drop updates when overloaded rather than queueing them.
Dense hotspots (airports, events): queue-based dispatch zones with first-in-first-out drivers.
Region boundaries: query neighbouring partitions near borders.
tradeoffs: Stale locations are acceptable; stale ride state is not, so the two use different stores.
Best ETA matching vs global optimisation over many rides (batch matching every few seconds can improve total wait).
City partitioning simplifies scaling but complicates trips that cross boundaries.

rubric.text: Sized the location update rate and kept hot locations in memory.
Used a geospatial index to find nearby drivers.
Prevented double assignment with conditional updates or locks.
Modelled the ride as an explicit state machine.
Ranked by ETA rather than straight-line distance.
Pushed live trip updates to both parties.
Partitioned by city and handled boundaries and hotspots.
Discussed batch vs greedy matching and load shedding.
